CONTRACT v3: only `title` (<=6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (<=140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Posture: destination-mobility partner — the lead story is that RSG's own peer-reviewed Al Wajh lagoon Marine Spatial Plan commits to electric-only marine vehicles, and Navier is the vessel class that fulfils that published commitment. Rendered respectfully — 'the commitment is published; the vessel now exists' — never as criticism; RSG's existing 13-vessel marine fleet renders only as their neutral published fact. Destination-internal corridors only; the 79-nm inter-destination leg and all unverified landings are roadmap items. No counterparty identities beyond published PIF/RSG facts, no program or fleet commitments, no launch dates, no NEOM/Sindalah (different developer — excluded entirely), no partnership claims with RSG or any resort brand. Access: unlisted/noindex per instruction (deviation from the Dubai gold master's public access — this is a named-counterparty destination page).

fn1.text: The peer-reviewed Marine Spatial Plan for the 2,081 km² Al Wajh lagoon conserves 58% of the marine area outright, holds development to a 5% footprint, and lists 'the use of electric-only marine and land vehicles to avoid pollution and noise' among its committed conservation measures.

fn2.text: The destination's published SIIG Model is a roadmap to a 30% net conservation gain by 2040, with priority zones covering corals, mangroves, seagrass, sea turtles, marine mammals and island birds.

fn3.text: The Red Sea spans 28,000 km² and more than 90 islands, with under 1% of the area developed, visitor numbers capped at 1 million a year to protect biodiversity, and the destination powered entirely by off-grid renewable energy — 760,000 solar panels and one of the world's largest battery storage systems.

fn4.text: Hotel counts are derived from the developer's published statements: eleven properties open today, five of them on Shura Island. The water-served outer islands hold 226 villas — St. Regis Red Sea (90), Nujuma, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve (63) and Shebara (73) — with counts as published by the brands and trade press.

fn5.text: No numeric speed limits are published for these waters. All trip times assume 25 knots in open lagoon water on marked transfer routes and 8 knots within half a nautical mile of every landing and across flagged conservation areas — a stated conservative planning assumption, not a claim about the rules. Distances are coordinate-derived.

fn6.text: AMAALA opened its first wave at Triple Bay: six resorts of roughly 650 keys, Marina Village, and a yacht club whose 10-hectare marina berths yachts up to 130 metres and hosts The Ocean Race Grand Finale 2027.

fn7.text: Red Sea International Airport handled roughly 130,000 passengers in 2025. Vessel-borne guests transfer about 20 km by road from the airport to the Turtle Bay jetty; the airport itself operates a seaplane terminal, not a marina.

fn8.text: Red Sea Global's mobility subsidiary, Coastal Transportation Services Company, runs guest and staff mobility across the destinations — a published marine fleet of 13 vessels, 145 electric vehicles and 170 charging stations — alongside Fly Red Sea, the Kingdom's first seaplane company.

copy.lead: This destination is not waiting to be convinced about electric water mobility. Red Sea Global's peer-reviewed Marine Spatial Plan for the Al Wajh lagoon lists electric-only marine and land vehicles among its committed conservation measures, caps visitors at one million a year, and conserves 58% of the lagoon's marine area outright.

copy.framing: One counterparty, one conversation. Red Sea Global is master developer and operator in its own destinations — it owns the landings, runs guest mobility, and publishes the conservation rules. The posture here is extension: a zero-emission foiling tier inside the mobility network the destination already operates.
copy.enable_track: License and land the vessels — every stop is an existing destination marina or resort jetty. Private capital finances the vessels; the ask is landing access and licensing, not money.
copy.operate_track: Contract the foiling tier the way guest transfers run today — per-guest transfer pricing inside the existing resort fee structure, scheduled alongside the destination's own mobility operation and counted toward its published conservation commitments.

operate_proof_points.proof: The destination's own mobility subsidiary runs integrated land, air and marine guest and staff transfers — a published marine fleet of 13 vessels, 145 electric vehicles and 170 charging stations, plus marina operations at both destinations.

The Kingdom's first seaplane company, built in-house for scheduled island transfers from the destination's own airports — this developer already creates new mobility modes when the destination needs them.

Electric-only marine vehicles are a committed conservation measure in the lagoon's Marine Spatial Plan, and the SIIG Model targets a 30% net conservation gain by 2040 — the standards a foiling electric tier is built to meet.

copy.headline: Conservation zones are the rules here.
copy.framing: The controlling rules in these waters are conservation zones, not posted speed limits — written for wake, wash, noise, pollution and wildlife disturbance. A foiling, electric vessel satisfies those purposes inherently.
copy.ask: Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows a zone's purpose is served, set corridor speeds zone by zone — at the destination's discretion, inside the licensing pathway that already exists.

expander.title: What zone-by-zone measurement unlocks
body: No numeric speed limits are published for these waters, so every time on this page assumes 25 knots in open lagoon water on marked transfer routes and 8 knots near every landing and across flagged conservation areas — a stated conservative assumption, not a claim about the rules. Inside its destinations the developer sets vessel operating practice; on the wider coast the Saudi Red Sea Authority licenses coastal tourism and navigation, and its published guide series defines the licensing pathway.

Where operating practice holds vessels slow to protect reef frontages, seagrass and turtle habitat from wake and noise, a foiling hull that produces almost neither may justify higher transit speeds — always at the destination's discretion, shown here only as what measurement could unlock, never in base times.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter over coral, seagrass and resort frontages are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 30 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.
